title: Which US states require sexual harassment training, and how often?
description: US state sexual harassment training laws in CA, NY, IL, CT, ME and DE compared by employer size, hours and frequency, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: There is no federal sexual harassment training mandate for private employers in the United States, but several states require it. As at November 2026, New York and Illinois require annual training from all employers; California requires training every two years from employers with five or more employees; Delaware every two years at 50 or more; Connecticut two hours within six months of hire at three or more; and Maine new-hire training at 15 or more.
keyTakeaways: The duty follows the employee's work location. A company based anywhere in the world must meet a state's rule for staff who work in that state.
Annual training for every employer, regardless of size: New York State (Labor Law 201-g) and Illinois (by December 31 each calendar year, from employers with one or more employees).
Every two years: California (5 or more employees; 2 hours for supervisors, 1 hour for others) and Delaware (50 or more employees in Delaware).

One-time or long-cycle training: Connecticut (3 or more employees; 2 hours within six months of hire; supplemental training at least every ten years) and Maine (15 or more employees; new employees within one year).

Thresholds count differently: California counts employees anywhere, Delaware counts employees in Delaware, and Connecticut applies its rule to Connecticut-based staff of employers with three or more employees at any location.
regulator: State agencies, including the California Civil Rights Department, New York State Department of Labor and Division of Human Rights, Illinois Department of Human Rights, Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities, Maine Department of Labor, and Delaware Department of Labor
appliesTo: Employers with employees working in California, New York, Illinois, Connecticut, Maine or Delaware, subject to each state's size threshold
Employers in New York City with 15 or more employees, or one or more domestic workers, for additional city requirements
Multinational and remote-first employers with even one employee in a state that has a low or no threshold

sections.heading: Is sexual harassment training required by federal law?

blocks.text: No general federal statute requires private employers to provide sexual harassment training; the specific training mandates come from states and some cities. Federal law prohibits workplace sexual harassment nationwide, and training is widely used as part of preventing it, but the duty to train on a schedule, for set hours, with set content, is a matter of state law.

For international employers this has a practical consequence: the obligation attaches to where an employee works. A company headquartered in Lisbon, Tokyo or Dubai with a single employee in Illinois must train that employee every year. The Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities gives a similar example: a Minnesota-based company with ten employees in Minnesota and one in Connecticut must train the Connecticut employee. This page covers only states whose requirements were checked against an official state source; the absence of a state from the table does not mean it has no rule.

sections.heading: How do the state requirements compare?

blocks.text: The six states below differ on employer size, hours, frequency, and who must be trained. Each row is drawn from the state's own statute or agency guidance, linked in the sections that follow.

blocks.text: The most demanding combination for a national employer is usually the strictest frequency (annual, from New York and Illinois) applied together with the most specific content and hour rules (California and Connecticut). A multistate employer can therefore run one annual program designed to meet all of them, then add state-specific modules. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What do California and New York require?

blocks.text: California requires training every two years from employers with five or more employees; New York requires annual training from every employer. The California Civil Rights Department's [employer FAQ](https://calcivilrights.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/32/2022/11/Sexual-Harassment-Prevention-Training-For-Employers-FAQ_ENG.pdf) (October 2025) states that under Government Code section 12950.1, nonsupervisory employees must receive one hour and supervisors two hours of training every two years, that the next training deadline is January 1, 2027, and that an employer must train its California-based employees "so long as it employs 5 or more employees anywhere." Records must be kept for at least two years.

New York [Labor Law section 201-g](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/LAB/201-G) requires every employer to adopt the state's model sexual harassment prevention policy or an equivalent, and to use the model training program or one that "equals or exceeds the minimum standards provided by such model training," which must be interactive and provided annually. The [New York City Commission on Human Rights](https://www.nyc.gov/site/cchr/law/sexual-harassment-training.page) adds city rules, including three-year record retention, a poster and a new-hire fact sheet for employers with 15 or more employees or one or more domestic workers. Both states are covered in depth in [California and New York harassment training requirements](/regulations/california-and-new-york-harassment-training).

Illinois requires every employer with one or more employees to train all employees every calendar year. The Illinois Department of Human Rights (IDHR) [training FAQs](https://dhr.illinois.gov/about-us/idhr-faqs/training-faqs.html) state: "As of January 1, 2020, employers are required to train every employee each calendar year. By December 31st of each calendar year, all employees must have been trained."

IDHR publishes a free model training. Employers may use a third-party provider or their own program if it meets the minimum standards in the Illinois Human Rights Act (section 2-109 for general employers). Restaurants and bars must also provide supplemental training meeting section 2-110. Employers must keep a record of all trainings and make it available for IDHR's review, and IDHR advises training new staff as soon as possible after hire. Failure to provide the annual training is a violation of the Act, and employees may file a charge with IDHR.

Connecticut requires two hours of interactive training for every employee of an employer with three or more employees, within six months of hire, with supplemental training at least every ten years. The Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities (CHRO) [FAQ](https://portal.ct.gov/chro/-/media/chro/sexual-harassment-prevention-training/sexual-harassment-faqs-english.pdf) explains that Public Acts 19-16 and 19-93, together the Time's Up Act, took effect on October 1, 2019.

If an employer has fewer than three employees, all supervisors must still receive two hours of training. CHRO's free online video satisfies the requirement. On format, CHRO states the training "must be in a format that allows participants to ask questions and receive answers," for example a live question and answer session or a way to submit questions and receive answers within a reasonable time. It may be recorded or online if it includes that interactive element.

sections.heading: What do Maine and Delaware require?

blocks.text: Maine requires new-hire training at 15 or more employees, and Delaware requires training every two years at 50 or more employees in Delaware. Under [26 MRSA section 807](https://legislature.maine.gov/statutes/26/title26sec807.html), employers in workplaces with 15 or more employees must conduct an education and training program for all new employees within one year of commencement of employment, with additional training for supervisory and managerial employees within one year. Training records must be kept for at least three years. Separately, every Maine employer must give all employees annual individual written notice covering, among other things, the definition of sexual harassment and the complaint process.

Under [19 Del. C. section 711A(g)](https://delcode.delaware.gov/title19/c007/sc02/index.html), employers with 50 or more employees in Delaware must provide interactive training to new employees within one year of starting and every two years after that, with additional interactive training for supervisors on the same cycle. The training must cover the illegality and definition of sexual harassment with examples, legal remedies and the complaint process, how to contact the Department of Labor, and the prohibition against retaliation. Applicants, independent contractors, and employees employed less than six months continuously do not have to be trained.

sections.heading: How can a multistate employer build one program that meets every state?

blocks.text: Build a single program to the strictest common standard, then layer state-specific content and records on top. The checklist below is illustrative and should be checked against each state's current text.

See [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) and [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each state's requirement as a set of obligations linked to work location and role, so one core course can carry state-specific modules and records. When a state changes its rule, the affected employees and content can be identified from those links. See [compliance programs](/programs/compliance).

faqs.q: Does a remote employee's home state determine the training requirement?
faqs.a: Generally, yes: the state rules attach to employees who work in the state. California's Civil Rights Department, for example, requires training for California-based employees of employers with five or more employees anywhere, and Connecticut's CHRO applies its rule to Connecticut-based staff. Employers should track each employee's work state.

faqs.q: Can one annual course satisfy every state?
faqs.a: It can, if it is designed to the strictest elements: annual frequency, at least two hours for supervisors and Connecticut staff, interactive questions and answers, and state-specific content such as agency contacts and remedies. Records must also meet the longest retention period that applies.

faqs.q: Does Illinois require training for new employees immediately?
faqs.a: Illinois requires all employees to be trained by December 31 of each calendar year. IDHR's FAQ advises employers to train new staff as soon as possible after hire or by the end-of-year deadline. Restaurants and bars have supplemental training requirements under section 2-110 of the Illinois Human Rights Act.

faqs.q: Are other states adding training mandates?
faqs.a: States change these laws periodically, and some cities add their own rules, as New York City does. This page lists only requirements verified on official state sources as at November 2026. Employers operating in states not listed should check that state's civil rights or labor agency directly.
